extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in cultural studies, ethics, and social issues
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the concepts, criteria, contexts, and contested evaluations used to identify or judge instances of cultural appropriation across arts, religion, fashion, language, sports, and other social domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition — adoption perceived as inappropriate or unacknowledged
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cultural appropriation is the adoption of an element or elements of culture or identity by members of another culture or identity in a manner perceived as inappropriate or unacknowledged."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charges typically arise when members of a dominant culture borrow from minority cultures. Includes adoption of religious and cultural traditions, customs, dance steps, fashion, symbols, language, history and music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant-versus-minority context
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation is often identified when members of a dominant culture borrow from minority cultures or from cultures subordinated in social, political, economic, or military status to the dominant culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations consider power imbalances and historical relations (colonialism, oppression). The same act may be assessed differently depending on whether the appropriator belongs to a historically dominant group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of cultural elements subject to appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural appropriation can include the adoption of religious and cultural traditions, customs, dance steps, fashion, symbols, language, history and music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article include iconography, tribal names/mascots, ceremonial items, tattoos, hairstyles, clothing, spiritual practices, slang/AAVE, and food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm via removal from original context (distortion/exoticization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents view appropriation as exploitative when cultural elements are lost or distorted as they are removed from their originating cultural contexts, reduced to 'exotic' fashion or toys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the practice divorces elements from their meaning, trivialises sacred or historical content, or presents them as kitsch—offending or erasing original cultural significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: EED framework — erasure, exploitation, denigration (Julia Serano)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serano defines cultural appropriation as problematic when it involves at least one of three interrelated harms: erasure, exploitation, or denigration (EED).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasure: ignoring or obscuring the voices/contexts of the original community. Exploitation: gaining material, symbolic, or commercial benefit without returning value. Denigration: treating borrowed elements as trivial, exotic, or mocking rather than respecting their meaning. Distinguishes harmful 'EED appropriation' from non-EED appropriation which may not inflict these harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exchange vs appropriation criterion (even playing field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual exchange happens on an 'even playing field', whereas appropriation involves pieces of an oppressed culture being taken out of context by people who have historically oppressed those they are taking from and who lack the cultural context to properly understand, respect, or utilise these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of reciprocity, consent, and balanced power relations to distinguish exchange from appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual knowledge and respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use without understanding or respect for the history and socio-historical circumstances of cultural forms increases the risk of perpetuating unequal power relations and misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations consider whether appropriators have taken care to recognize specific socio-historical significance and whether they acknowledge origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred/status items and earned rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Wearing or using items of deep cultural significance and status that traditionally must be earned (e.g., Native American war bonnet) without having earned the right is considered appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the item is sacred or tied to earned social roles; using such items as costume or fashion is flagged as erasure and disrespect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and competence in adopting ritual practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-members conducting religious or ceremonial practices (e.g., sweat lodge, vision quest, ayahuasca ceremonies) may create serious safety risks and harm when lacking years of training and cultural immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider practical safety outcomes (injuries, deaths) in addition to cultural disrespect; improper enactment can be both physically dangerous and culturally appropriative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialisation and lack of compensation/acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation is criticized when designers, brands, or individuals commercialise cultural heritage, profiting without consent, acknowledgement, or compensation to the originating communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of financial gain by appropriators, absence of benefit-return mechanisms, or failure to credit source communities (e.g., fashion lines, brand names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective intellectual property and rights of indigenous cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenous cultural expressions and traditional knowledge are framed as collective resources that should be governed collectively; individual members cannot unilaterally give away rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and policy evaluations should consider collective ownership, potential treaty recognition, and mechanisms to protect communal cultural property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconography divorced from meaning (kitsch and misrepresentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying iconography (tattoos, characters, art styles) and wearing them without regard for original cultural significance may be considered appropriation when divorced from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether symbols are being used superficially as decoration or novelty, and whether that usage offends people who venerate and wish to preserve the tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mascots and stereotyping — reinforcing colonial dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Using tribal names or images as mascots is a common example of appropriation that can cause harm by reinforcing colonial dynamics and perpetuating stereotypical perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether such uses maintain superiority narratives, constitute dysconscious racism, or contribute to hostile/abusive environments (e.g., sports teams controversies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion-specific considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In fashion, appropriation debates focus on whether designers understand histories behind clothing, whether appropriation violates shared intellectual property without consent, and whether it trivialises heritage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider designer intent, consultation with source communities, the presence/absence of acknowledgement or profit-sharing, and public reactions (apologies, backlash).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and branding sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using culturally specific names (e.g., 'Kimono' for a shapewear line) can provoke backlash if perceived as trivialising or misusing a culturally significant term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess responsiveness to critiques (e.g., changing names, issuing apologies) and whether community perspectives were considered before branding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and hairstyle appropriation (including 'blackfishing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting looks associated with particular racial/ethnic groups (braids, dreadlocks, tanning/makeup to appear darker) can be seen as appropriation when it takes aesthetics without experiencing associated societal harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether such adoption robs opportunities, amounts to deception, resembles historical practices like blackface, or lets appropriators avoid negative consequences experienced by the source group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language appropriation (AAVE and slang)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of African American Vernacular English (AAVE) or slang by outsiders on social media can be perceived as intrusion into cultural identity and as increasing power imbalances between linguistic majority and minority groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether usage respects origins, acknowledges source communities, or functions as casual commodification of vernaculars without appreciation or credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and genre appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres and styles (e.g., Black music forms) appropriated by other groups raise concerns about lack of acknowledgement and financial compensation to originators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical misattribution of origins, revenue distribution, and whether appropriation obscures creators' contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food/cuisine appropriation and 'food colonialism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebranding or claiming dishes associated with another group (e.g., presenting hummus/falafel as 'Israeli' without acknowledging Palestinian origins) can be framed as erasing identity and creating new narratives tied to territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate politics of naming, historical displacement, and whether claiming of dishes serves profit or national narratives that erase origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and scholarly criteria — distinguishing cultural change modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars note the need to distinguish appropriation from acculturation, assimilation, diffusion, and other modes of cultural change to properly assess outcomes and meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical/contextual analysis to determine whether an instance is structural inversion of assimilation or a different process; consider trade routes, imperial histories, and documented exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for non-harmful borrowing (non-EED appropriation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all borrowing is inherently oppressive; non-EED appropriation occurs where adoption does not result in erasure, exploitation, or denigration and may support or amplify minority communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for positive outcomes such as amplification, respectful collaboration, crediting, compensation, and active support of source communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms of the concept as evaluative cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue the concept is sometimes misunderstood, misapplied, arbitrary, or inhibitive of artistic freedom; some say it lacks conceptual coherence or wrongfully treats cultural acts as property crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the label, consider debates about essentializing culture, artistic freedom, freedom of expression, and whether claims rest on coherent standards rather than ad-hoc policing of interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and ethical complexity in protecting cultural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying intellectual property frameworks to cultural appropriation is legally and ethically complex because some cultural 'properties' belong to groups too large to operationalize consent procedures; blanket rejection of borrowing may be harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy responses should weigh benefits of cultural mixing, difficulty of enforcing collective consent, and potential negative consequences of overly broad prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment indicators used in public controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Public controversies are often evaluated by indicators such as community protests, legal decisions/policies (e.g., NCAA mascot policy), public apologies, removal of items/names, and institutional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these observable signals (e.g., team name changes, product renaming/removal, consultation agreements with tribes) as part of holistic judgment about harm and appropriate remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and community consultation as remedial criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses that involve consultation with source communities, explicit support/agreements, or restitution (e.g., waivers, tribal approvals, profit-sharing) are presented as antidotes to appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether appropriators sought and obtained consent, engaged ongoing consultation, and provided recognition or material benefit to origin communities.
